title: Chloroplast
summary: A chloroplast is the green food-making organelle inside plant cells. It captures energy from sunlight and uses it with water and carbon dioxide to make sugar - powering the plant through photosynthesis. Explore its internal discs and green pigment.

compareCandidate.label: Chloroplast vs. mitochondrion
compareCandidate.description: Chloroplasts capture sunlight to make sugar (food), a job only plants and algae do. Mitochondria release energy from food, a job done in all eukaryotic cells. One builds food, the other spends it.

processes: Photosynthesis: making sugar from light, water, and CO2
Using plants as the plant's food maker
plainLanguageExplanation: The chloroplast is the place where a plant makes its own food. It is green because of a pigment called chlorophyll inside it that captures sunlight energy. Inside, chloroplasts contain stacks of flat discs called thylakoids, and a fluid space around them called the stroma. Using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide, the chloroplast makes sugar (the plant's food) and releases oxygen. Because it captures and uses light, the chloroplast is the organelle at the center of a leaf and of the whole plant's nutrition.

keyFacts.label: Where

keyFacts.label: Green

keyFacts.label: Only in plants

whyItMatters: Chloroplasts are the microscopic powerhouses where plants turn sunlight into food - food that feeds almost every living thing on Earth, and that produces the oxygen we breathe. They are why a green leaf is the kitchen of a plant.
tagline: The green food factory inside cells
didYouKnow: A single leaf cell can contain many chloroplasts, and there can be hundreds of thousands in a leaf, all using sunlight to make sugar.
